stem: In a class of 60 students, 35 play cricket, 25 play football, and 10 play both. How many students play exactly one of the two games?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Only cricket = 35 - 10 = 25; only football = 25 - 10 = 15; exactly one game = 25 + 15 = 40.
This is n(A union B) = 35 + 25 - 10 = 50, which counts students who play at least one game, not exactly one.
This comes from 35 + 25 - 10 - 20 = 30, incorrectly subtracting the overlap twice from the union instead of applying the correct formula.
This returns the total class size n(U) = 60, not the count of students playing exactly one sport.

explanation: Only cricket = 35 - 10 = 25. Only football = 25 - 10 = 15. Exactly one game = 25 + 15 = 40. Equivalently, n(A union B) - 2*n(A intersect B) = 50 - 10*2 = 30... correction: 50 - 10 = 40 uses union minus intersection once, which removes the double-counted overlap entirely. So exactly-one = n(A union B) - n(A intersect B) = 50 - 10 = 40.

explanation_sections.punchline: Exactly one game equals the union minus the intersection: those in both groups are removed from the exclusively-one count.
explanation_sections.approach: State the formula: exactly one = n(A) + n(B) - 2*n(A intersect B) = 35 + 25 - 20 = 40. This strips the overlap from both individual counts.
explanation_sections.lesson: At-least-one = union; exactly-one = n(A) + n(B) - 2*n(A intersect B). Memorise the factor of 2 on the intersection.
explanation_sections.timing: 55 s. The trap is 50 (the union), which counts at-least-one, not exactly-one.
